summary: Lists numbers assigned for networks, protocols and related identifiers on the ARPA Internet. Such lists were reissued as assignments changed. This RFC is historic. Replaced by RFC 820.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone book for early internet services and networks. A newer edition replaced it.

questions: class a class b class c networks
subtitle: Updated registry of network and protocol identifiers for the growing ARPA Internet.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, the registry of assigned numbers from RFC 770 needed updating with new addresses, protocols and port assignments.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 790 publishes assigned values: IPv4 address classes (A, B, C) for different network sizes, IP protocol numbers, protocol versions, and port/socket numbers, again centrally managed by Jon Postel.
tldr.outcome: The Internet gained a structured addressing scheme with three address classes. Historic; RFC 820 replaced it with further updates.

today: RFC 790 is Historic. RFC 820 replaced it with further updates. The IPv4 address classes defined here remained the standard until CIDR notation was introduced.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: This RFC documents assigned numbers for the ARPA Internet as of 1981, updated from RFC 770. It lists network numbers, protocol versions, protocol types, ports and other identifiers. The management remains centralized under Jon Postel at USC Information Sciences Institute. This edition introduces the IPv4 address classes that would become fundamental to Internet addressing for decades.
sections.plainLanguage: The updated directory of Internet numbers and services, with a new system for dividing Internet addresses into three sizes.

sections.title: IPv4 Address Classes
sections.content: RFC 790 defines three address classes in the 32-bit IPv4 address space: Class A has a 7-bit network number and 24-bit local address (allowing 128 networks); Class B has a 14-bit network number and 16-bit local address (allowing 16,384 networks); and Class C has a 21-bit network number and 8-bit local address (allowing over 2 million networks). Each class uses different leading bits to signal its type. Large organizations would use Class A, medium ones Class B, and Class C was for smaller networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet addresses come in three sizes: Class A for huge networks, Class B for medium ones, and Class C for small ones. The leading bits tell you which size it is.

sections.title: Protocols and Ports
sections.content: The RFC assigns protocol numbers for the IP protocol field (TCP is 6, UDP is 17, and others), port numbers for well-known services like Telnet (23), SMTP (25), and FTP (21), and Internet protocol versions. These tables grew from RFC 770 as the Internet expanded with new protocols and services. Internet addresses are now described in three formats corresponding to the address classes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every protocol and service gets a number. FTP is port 21, email is port 25, and so on, so computers know what service is handling the data.

references.text: Feinler, E. and J. Postel, eds., "ARPANET Protocol Handbook," NIC 7104, 1980.
